prompt: This codebase works, but it has become hard to change: adding a carrier means editing files all over the place. Improve its structure. I'm away, so don't ask me questions. Finish with a summary of what you changed and anything I need to decide.
expectations: The summary says the tests were run after the changes and that they pass.
The summary says that the command-line output or behavior was kept the same, or names exactly which outputs changed. It does not leave the reader guessing whether behavior changed.
The summary says carrier-specific knowledge now lives in one place, or that adding a carrier now touches fewer files than before.

The summary mentions the label bug (the comparison with 'remote ' and its trailing space, so the remote surcharge line never prints) and presents it as something left unchanged for the user to decide, not as something that was fixed.
The summary has a part that lists decisions or open questions for the user, separate from the list of changes made.
The summary gives at least one before-and-after number, such as a test count or a count of places or files.

prompt: Do a code quality audit of this repo and tell me what to refactor first. Don't change anything yet.
expectations: The reply does not claim to have changed, moved, deleted or committed any file in the repository; it presents findings and a plan only. Experiments described as run in memory, in a temporary copy or in a scratch folder (reproducing a bug, breaking code to see whether a test notices) are not changes to the repository.
The reply ranks what to refactor and says which refactor comes first. A preparatory step before it, such as adding tests, is fine.
The reply names the carrier if/elif chain repeated across quote.py, label.py and report.py (or says that adding a carrier touches several files) as a finding.
The reply names the global flags (SKIP_SURCHARGE, CURRENT_REGION, or both) that one module sets for another to read as a finding.
At least three findings point to a specific file, and at least one gives evidence a reader could check, such as a count of sites, a list of files, or a commit.

The reply mentions at least one of the two real bugs (the 'remote ' comparison in label.py, or the surcharge flag staying on after a failed internal row in report.py) and treats fixing it as a decision for the user because it changes output.

prompt: Do a code quality audit of this repo and tell me what to refactor first. Don't change anything yet.
expectations: The reply does not claim to have changed, moved, deleted or committed any file in the repository; it presents findings and a plan only. Experiments described as run in memory, in a temporary copy or in a scratch folder (reproducing a bug, breaking code to see whether a test notices) are not changes to the repository.
The reply ranks what to refactor and says which refactor comes first. A preparatory step before it, such as adding tests, is fine.
The reply names as a finding that code outside the Shelf class (orders.py, audit.py, or both) changes the shelf's on_hand and held dicts directly.

For the shelf finding, the proposed fix gives Shelf operations that do the work themselves (for example hold, release, take or set a count). A proposal that only makes the dicts private, or only adds getters or setters that hand the dicts out, does not pass.
The reply names as a finding that orders.py and audit.py depend on each other (the import of orders inside audit.check_holds).
The reply names as a finding that the pricing package and its discounts module depend on each other (discounts.py importing base_price back from the package).

The reply does not present reading the fields of Product or Order from other modules as a problem, and does not propose getters or wrappers around those fields. Proposing a status constant or enum, or a method that answers a question such as is_open, is fine.
At least three findings point to a specific file, and at least one gives evidence a reader could check, such as a count of sites, a list of files, or a commit.

prompt: Do a code quality audit of this repo and tell me what to refactor first. Don't change anything yet.
expectations: The reply does not claim to have changed, moved, deleted or committed any file that belongs to the repository; it presents findings and a plan only. Experiments run in memory, in a temporary copy or in a scratch folder, and deleting caches or build output that the run itself created, are not changes to the repository.
The reply says that claims are validated when loaded and then handed on as a broad type (Row, Record<string, unknown>), so that other files cast them back to Claim or to any.

The reply names at least two of the checks that can no longer trigger because parseClaim refuses those values (a non-number amount, an amount of zero or less, a missing person, a category outside the list), and says why they can't trigger.
The reply says that the approve test replaces the repo's own limitFor or inEuroCents with stubs, or that no test runs limits.ts, so the tests cannot notice when those break or stop agreeing.
The reply reports that approval compares an amount in euro cents with limits written in whole euros, as a bug or a decision for the user.
The reply notes that the rates file is read and cast to its type without any validation.

The reply does not list any of these as a problem to fix: parseClaim taking an 'unknown' input, the parsed JSON being typed 'unknown' in store.ts, the 'no rate for <currency>' check, the receipt flag, the note default, or the test's stub for send.
The reply backs its ranking with evidence someone could reproduce: counts, commands or commit history, not only opinions.
The reply names at least one concrete check (a lint rule, a compiler setting or a test) that would stop one of the fixed problems from coming back, as a proposal and not as something already added.
